# Introduction

Quantum mechanics is the rigid ground of hadron spectroscopy. A Hamiltonian
gives a spectrum, its eigenvectors give matrix elements, and mixing changes
both the identity of a state and the transitions it can make. Whatever else is
said about a resonance --- its assignment, its width, its partner --- eventually
reduces to those operations, and a spectroscopist who cannot carry them out for
a given model is reading its predictions rather than using them.

The relativized quark model of Godfrey and Isgur [@godfrey1985], hereafter GI,
carries out those operations across light and heavy mesons, "from the pion to
the upsilon," within a single soft-QCD Hamiltonian. One fixed set of parameters
produces the masses, and afterwards the couplings, of essentially the whole
meson landscape. Four decades later it is still the baseline against which new
states are judged.

It is also, in practice, unavailable. The relativistic smearing, the
momentum-dependent operator factors, and the isoscalar annihilation machinery
are specified semiquantitatively, spread across the main text and Appendix A,
and the spectra themselves are published as figures rather than tables. To use
the model at all you must first rebuild it.

So I looked for a version somebody had already built. An extensive search of
GitHub and the wider open-source ecosystem turns up numerical libraries ---
SciPy, PETSc/SLEPc, Eigen --- and generic one-dimensional Schrödinger and
Salpeter solvers, and nothing that encodes the GI Hamiltonian, its
mass-dependent smearing and momentum-factor operators, or its tensor,
antisymmetric spin--orbit, and annihilation mixing. More broadly, there is no
open implementation of constituent quark-model meson spectroscopy at all.
Every reproduction therefore begins by reconstructing the Hamiltonian and its
numerical conventions from the paper trail, and ends in a private directory.
That absence, sitting under a field that treats the quantum-mechanical
calculation as its foundation, is the practical demand this project answers.

GIModel.jl recomputes the GI spectrum from the published ingredients, taking
Table II verbatim and fitting nothing. @sec-computation sets out what the paper
asks you to compute and how the packages are organized around it;
@sec-implementation describes how the calculation was built, the corrections
that were needed, and what the reproduction currently rests on; @sec-usage
describes using it, as a calculation and as teaching material; @sec-conclusion
collects what is settled and what comes next. Throughout, the 1985 paper is the
authority and the code is a claim about it.

# Computation and architecture {#sec-computation}

## The model Hamiltonian

GI start from a rest-frame equation with a relativistic kinetic term,
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:schrodinger}
H\,|\Psi\rangle = (H_0 + V)\,|\Psi\rangle = E\,|\Psi\rangle ,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kinetic}
H_0 = \sqrt{p^2 + m_1^2} + \sqrt{p^2 + m_2^2},
\end{equation}
```
with $V=V(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{r})$ momentum dependent and
$\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p}_1=-\mathbf{p}_2$. In the nonrelativistic limit $V$
reduces to the familiar sum of confinement, hyperfine, and spin--orbit terms.
The spin-independent piece combines a linear Lorentz-scalar term with a
Coulomb-type one-gluon exchange,
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conf}
H^{\text{conf}}_{ij}
  = -\Big[\tfrac34 c + \tfrac34 b r - \frac{\alpha_s(r)}{r}\Big]\,
    \mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j ,
\end{equation}
```
with $\langle \mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j\rangle = -4/3$ in a meson; the
color hyperfine interaction supplies the contact and tensor pieces,
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hyp}
H^{\text{hyp}}_{ij} = -\frac{\alpha_s(r)}{m_i m_j}
  \Big[\tfrac{8\pi}{3}\,\mathbf{S}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{S}_j\,\delta^3(\mathbf{r})
  + \frac{1}{r^3}\,S_{ij}\Big]\mathbf{F}_i\!\cdot\!\mathbf{F}_j ,
\end{equation}
```
with $S_{ij}$ the usual tensor operator; the spin--orbit interaction splits
into a color-magnetic and a Thomas-precession part. A separate gluon-annihilation term $H_A$ contributes
only in self-conjugate isoscalar channels.

As GI themselves stress, `Eq.~\eqref{eq:hyp}`{=latex} and its spin--orbit companions
are more singular than $r^{-2}$ and are illegal operators in
`Eq.~\eqref{eq:schrodinger}`{=latex} as written.
The resolution is the paper's Appendix A, which is where the reproduction work
actually lives.

## Relativization: smearing and momentum factors

Two things happen there. First, the relative coordinate is *smeared* over
distances of order the inverse quark masses,
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:smear}
\rho_{ij}(\mathbf{r}'-\mathbf{r})
  = \frac{\sigma_{ij}^3}{\pi^{3/2}}\,
    e^{-\sigma_{ij}^2(\mathbf{r}'-\mathbf{r})^2},
\end{equation}
```
with a mass-dependent width $\sigma_{ij}(\sigma_0,s)$, which tames the
short-distance singularities and makes the operators legal. Second, the
coefficients acquire a dependence on the quark momenta: mass factors $m^{-1}$
are promoted to operator factors built from $E_i=(p^2+m_i^2)^{1/2}$, so that
the light-quark hyperfine term saturates to a finite $m\to0$ limit controlled
by $\langle p^{-1}\rangle$ instead of diverging.

Concretely, the central Coulomb and confinement terms become their smeared
forms $\widetilde G(r)$ and $\widetilde S(r)$, and the Coulomb operator is
dressed with a Hermitian momentum sandwich,
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sandwich}
G' = A(p)\,\widetilde G\,A(p),
\qquad A(p) = \Big(1 + \tfrac{p^2}{E_1 E_2}\Big)^{1/2},
\end{equation}
```
with the same construction, at the side exponents $\tfrac12+\epsilon_i$ of
Table II, applied to the contact, tensor, and spin--orbit kernels. Those
kernels are themselves built from derivatives of the *smeared* central
functions. Getting the ordering of these operations right, and keeping it right
in two different numerical representations, turned out to be most of the
project.

The strong coupling is a frozen sum of Gaussians,
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alphaq}
\alpha_s(Q^2) = 0.25\,e^{-Q^2} + 0.15\,e^{-Q^2/10} + 0.20\,e^{-Q^2/1000},
\end{equation}
```
with $Q$ in GeV and $\alpha_s^{\text{crit}}=0.60$, which becomes a
coordinate-space error-function profile convenient for convolving with
`Eq.~\eqref{eq:smear}`{=latex}. In self-conjugate isoscalars, $q\bar q$ annihilates through gluons
($n=2$ for $C=+$, $n=3$ for $C=-$), and the channel-coupling element
```{=latex}
\begin{align}\label{eq:ann16}
A(^{2S+1}L_J)_{ji} = {}& 4\pi(2L{+}1)\,A(^{2S+1}L_J) \nonumber \\
  &\times \Big[\frac{\alpha_s(M_j^2)\alpha_s(M_i^2)}{\pi^2}\Big]^{n/2}
  \frac{S_L(\Psi_j)S_L(\Psi_i)}{m_i m_j}
\end{align}
```
carries a strength $A(^{2S+1}L_J)$ fixed per channel, the channel masses $M_j$
in the coupling, and a dependence on the wavefunction near the origin through
$S_L(\Psi_i)$. That
dependence makes the isoscalars the sharpest test of whether the wavefunctions
are right, not merely the energies.

## The paper's three-stage algorithm

The harmonic-oscillator (HO) basis was not a stylistic choice in 1985. It was
the practical route through an operator that depends on both position and
momentum: oscillator functions have tractable representations in both spaces,
and Appendix A inserts intermediate states to assemble products of the
corresponding matrix elements. The procedure has three stages. The relativized
Hamiltonian is diagonalized in a large HO basis within fixed $|jm;ls\rangle$
sectors, the basis being enlarged until convergence. The smaller mass matrices
generated by the off-diagonal tensor
($^3L_J\!\leftrightarrow\!{}^3L'_J$) and antisymmetric spin--orbit
($^3L_J\!\leftrightarrow\!{}^1L_J$, unequal masses only) couplings are then
diagonalized in the basis of those eigenvectors. Finally, self-conjugate
isoscalars acquire the annihilation matrix of `Eq.~\eqref{eq:ann16}`{=latex}.

## Inputs

The parameters are GI Table II, taken verbatim (`Table~\ref{tab:params}`{=latex}). These
constants, the $\alpha_s$ form of `Eq.~\eqref{eq:alphaq}`{=latex}, and the paper's
reference masses
are the only inputs; nothing is fitted here.

```{=latex}
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{GI Table II parameters, used verbatim. The tensor exponent is the
paper's $\epsilon_f$ (code \texttt{epsilon\_t}).}
\label{tab:params}
\begin{tabular}{llr}
\toprule
Quantity & Symbol & Value \\
\midrule
Light quark mass & $\tfrac12(m_u+m_d)$ & $220$ MeV \\
Strange mass & $m_s$ & $419$ MeV \\
Charm mass & $m_c$ & $1628$ MeV \\
Bottom mass & $m_b$ & $4977$ MeV \\
String tension & $b$ & $0.18$ GeV$^2$ \\
Constant & $c$ & $-253$ MeV \\
Frozen coupling & $\alpha_s^{\text{crit}}$ & $0.60$ \\
QCD scale & $\Lambda$ & $200$ MeV \\
Smearing width & $\sigma_0$ & $1.80$ GeV \\
Smearing exponent & $s$ & $1.55$ \\
Contact factor & $\epsilon_c$ & $-0.168$ \\
Tensor factor & $\epsilon_f$ & $+0.025$ \\
Vector spin--orbit & $\epsilon_{\text{so}(V)}$ & $-0.035$ \\
Scalar spin--orbit & $\epsilon_{\text{so}(S)}$ & $+0.055$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
```

GI quote an expected accuracy of $25$ MeV for light-quark mesons and $10$ MeV
for heavy-quark systems, dominated by neglected coupled-channel shifts and by
the schematic relativization. That is the standard the reproduction is measured
against, and it is worth separating early from a solver tolerance, which is a
statement about arithmetic rather than about physics.

## Package architecture

Two packages divide the work along the line that matters: GIModel computes,
GIPaper compares. GIModel knows nothing about the 1985 figures. A meson is
built from quark flavors, the levels to solve are named as explicit
$n\,^{2S+1}L_J$ multiplets, and `compute_spectrum` returns a `Spectrum` whose
states carry their contribution breakdowns and the provenance of every mixing
transformation applied to them. GIPaper owns the digitized reference data, maps
reference rows to mesons without fallback masses, runs the comparison, applies
the paper's Table III prescriptions for the isoscalar channels, and writes the
residual reports.
Nothing from the paper leaks into the calculation, so a residual can never be
manufactured by the layer that reports it.

Inside GIModel the same principle separates the model from its discretization.
`GIParameters` is grouped by physical aspect, one substruct per section of the
parameter file, and describes the Hamiltonian only. The choice of numerical
method lives on the solver --- a finite-difference (FD) or an oscillator
implementation of a common `RadialSolver` interface --- so switching method
does not rebuild the physics object, and the two methods can be run against
each other on identical inputs. Wavefunctions follow the same pattern: mesh
waves and oscillator waves are distinct types behind one wave interface, with
the norms, overlaps, and expectation values written once against that
interface. Momentum-space waves exist alongside them, which is what makes the
Appendix-A momentum factors expressible in their own representation instead of
through a mesh approximation.

# Implementation {#sec-implementation}

## From finite differences to the oscillator basis

I did not start with the paper's method. An FD radial calculation was the
easier foothold: grid values, explicit operator matrices, and contribution
plots gave something to look at directly, term by term, when nothing yet
worked. That was the right first move and the wrong final answer. Once the FD
spectrum stood up, its independence became the lever for going back to native
HO matrix elements, and then to the paper's own order of diagonalization and
mixing. The sequence was FD to HO, with comparison at every step.

The intermediate stage was the most instructive, because it looked finished
when it was not. Representing a wave in an HO expansion does not by itself
reproduce the paper's algorithm; native operator assembly, full fixed-sector
diagonalization, and the later mixing stages all still had to be recovered
individually. The native HO path now evaluates position- and
momentum-dependent factors in their own representations following Appendix A,
optimizes the oscillator scale, and enlarges the basis until every requested
energy passes a stated convergence test --- currently $0.1$ MeV over two
consecutive refinements, supplemented by wave-overlap diagnostics and
wave-sensitive audits. FD remains as an independent comparator, which is a
better role for it than the headline.

## Corrections that taught physics

The instructive part of the work was not the code that ran. It was the code
that ran *and was wrong*, and what it took to notice.

**Normalization and relative phase.** A diagonal Rayleigh quotient is unchanged
when its input vector is rescaled; a bare off-diagonal overlap is not. So
comparing sampled FD waves with reconstructed HO waves demanded a common
physical normalization, and without it perfectly matching diagonal results
happily coexisted with badly wrong mixing matrix elements. The fix is recorded
in commit `a987862`. The HO phase-convention correction in `9ff437b` is the
same lesson from the other side: an individual eigenvector has an arbitrary
phase, but every operator and every mixed-state composition must transform
consistently with whatever phase was chosen. Both are statements about physics
that arrived as implementation failures.

**A converged approximation can still be the wrong calculation.** A
nonperturbative solve that was unavailable in one path had been quietly falling
back to a first-order shift. Commit `eef789b` made that case fail loudly
instead. The later fixed-sector work (`b9d3474`) put the full diagonal spin
interactions into the Hamiltonian *before* solving it, rather than adding them
afterwards. Recovering the masses was not enough: the spin-distorted
wavefunctions have to reach the decay and annihilation observables too, which
is exactly where a first-order shortcut stops being invisible. The completion
in `78a3d76` also removed extra spin-strength bridge factors once the literal
Appendix-A coefficients were correct.

**Convergence certifies less than it appears to.** Commit `8655d68` removed the
mesh from the HO Appendix-A assembly, and `39ee9c8` made adaptive basis
refinement a production requirement rather than a diagnostic. Energy
convergence still had to be complemented by tests of origin-sensitive
functionals and of the final mixed-state observables: an energy can be stable
to $0.1$ MeV while $S_L(\Psi)$ in `Eq.~\eqref{eq:ann16}`{=latex} is still moving. The independent FD
certification in `bdd65d8` supplied a second numerical route with its own
spacing and domain checks, but agreement between two routes became evidence
about the physics only once each route's representations and approximations
were pinned down.

**Verification infrastructure can hide the mistake.** Commit `959fdb0`
corrected a scorecard that was faithfully reporting the *previous* verification
run, and `2fd3fd7` restored FD/HO audits that had drifted outside the gate. A
correct-looking report that does not describe the code under inspection is
worse than no report, and keeping the reference comparison and its generation
path explicit belongs to the physics rather than to the housekeeping around it.

## Agent-assisted development

Much of the work was carried out with coding agents, and the git history
records its whole shape: extraction from the paper, implementation, autonomous
iterations, physics audits, repairs, and eventually teaching material. The
paper, the numerical checks, and my own reading supplied the criteria for
accepting any of it.

The failure modes above are the reason the criteria mattered. Plausible code,
passing local tests, and a reassuring residual could all coexist with a missing
physical operation. What worked was the corrective loop: a discrepancy raised a
question about normalization, operator staging, or provenance; the question
sent me back to the paper or to an independent calculation; the answer changed
both the code and the explanation of it. The commit identifiers above are
navigation anchors into that record --- the changes and their audits are the
evidence, not the commit titles.

## Provenance and current status

GIPaper keeps a manifest of paper units with links to code, tests, reference
sources, and residual reports: the detailed record of what has been computed
and compared. Reference data keep their origin, whether a printed table or a
digitized figure. Parameter provenance is tracked with the same care, because
taking the paper's inputs, repeating a fit the paper performed, and calibrating
a diagnostic control against reference targets are three different operations,
and only the first two are predictions. The reports label which is which, so a
control cannot quietly become evidence.

One compact example of the present state: the photon audit gives a transition
magnetic moment, in nuclear magnetons, of $\mu/\mu_N=+0.688$ for
$\rho\to\pi\gamma$ against the printed $+0.69$, and
$-1.200$ for $K^{*0}\to K^0\gamma$ against $-1.20$, from the checked-in audit
of September 7, 2026. The $\rho$ row is also the row GI used to fit a
relativization exponent, so its agreement tests the reconstructed pipeline
rather than supplying an independent prediction --- the distinction the
provenance labels exist to preserve. Other transitions probe different flavor
weights, wavefunctions, and cancellations, and are the more interesting test.

The spectrum and its mixing stages are reproduced. Complete accounting of the
Table VI photon-decay rows and the characterization of their residuals are
still open, and some mixing- and cancellation-sensitive quantities retain
visible discrepancies. The audit files, not this report, are where that
boundary is authoritative.

# Usage {#sec-usage}

## From a question to a number

```{=latex}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
% Replace the box with:
% \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/pipeline.png}
\fbox{\begin{minipage}[c][3.1cm][c]{0.97\textwidth}\centering\itshape\small
reserved --- pipeline diagram: meson and level selection, radial solve,
fine-structure and mixing stages, physical states, observables and comparison
\end{minipage}}
\caption{From a meson to a spectrum and a decay. Flavors and the requested
$n\,^{2S+1}L_J$ multiplets enter on the left; the radial solver returns channel
solutions and waves; the fine-structure, mixing, and annihilation stages
assemble physical states with explicit composition; observables and the
comparison layer close the chain. Each arrow is an inspectable intermediate.}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure*}
```

The point of the architecture is that an answer can be taken apart, stage by
stage (`Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}`{=latex}). In the
model a rest-frame mass is an eigenvalue of the Hamiltonian, whose kinetic part
is `Eq.~\eqref{eq:kinetic}`{=latex} and whose remainder is the structure of
@sec-computation. When
configurations mix, a physical state is
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed}
|\Psi\rangle=\sum_a c_a|\psi_a\rangle,
\end{equation}
```
with signed coefficients and explicit flavor content, and a transition is a
coherent sum,
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coherent}
\langle\Psi_f|O|\Psi_i\rangle
 =\sum_{a,b}c_{f,a}^{*}c_{i,b}
   \langle\psi_{f,a}|O|\psi_{i,b}\rangle.
\end{equation}
```
Writing it out is the quickest way to see why a mixing *probability* cannot
predict a decay: the relative phases can enhance or cancel. A width needs the
decay operator, the normalization, and the kinematics as well.

The package exposes those stages in that order. A spectrum contains
identifiable states; a state resolves into physical components; components lead
to solver-native waves; waves lead to radial matrix elements; the comparison
layer relates the result to a printed number. Which quantity is an input, which
is computed, and which is a reference value stays visible at every step. That
also makes conversational use of the model reasonable: a language model can
turn a physics question into a package calculation and explain the objects that
come back, while the numbers come from executing the code and carry their
parameters, labels, solver settings, and convergence information with them.

## Learning track and notebooks

The reproduction turned into teaching material, because the questions the code
forced me to answer are the questions a student has anyway. The theory course
is nine sheets: radial quantum mechanics, angular momentum and meson quantum
numbers, variational and semirelativistic methods, confinement and the running
coupling, relativization and smearing, spin fine structure, mixing, decay
observables, and the complete spectrum algorithm. Every problem has a worked
solution and a short concept check. A computational-discovery sheet starts the
bridge to numerical work; the full hands-on course is still ahead.

Each piece has its own job. The paper gives the original model and its
reasoning. The course slows the derivations down and makes you do them. The
notebooks make the assumptions adjustable and the consequences immediate.

Pluto, Julia's reactive notebook environment, suits the last of those:
executable cells, dependencies that re-run on change,
mathematical prose, controls, and results that redraw when a mass or a solver
setting changes. Live documentation and linked docstrings make a notebook an
entry point into the package rather than a demonstration beside it, and the
documentation graph links the public operations explicitly, with a static link
audit checking that the path from any explanation to the next numerical
question exists. The adaptive HO notebook turns the convergence question of
@sec-implementation into the lesson: it follows the oscillator scale and the
basis refinements, shows the energies settling, and asks why a curve that looks
flat still needs a criterion --- and why energy convergence does not certify
every wave-sensitive observable.

## Exploring the model


```{=latex}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
% Replace the box with:
% \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/meson_structure.png}
\fbox{\begin{minipage}[c][3.4cm][c]{0.97\textwidth}\centering\itshape\small
reserved --- meson internal structure: three-dimensional densities
$|R_{nL}(r)Y_{Lm}(\theta,\phi)|^2$ for a radial and an orbital series
\end{minipage}}
\caption{Internal structure of the computed states. Three-dimensional
densities $|R_{nL}(r)\,Y_{Lm}(\theta,\phi)|^2$ built from the solver's own
radial waves: a radial series showing the growth of nodes, and an orbital
series showing the angular shape. The same solutions that produce the masses
produce these pictures.}
\label{fig:structure}
\end{figure*}
```

The heavy-quark notebook varies a constituent heavy-quark mass continuously
while the shared interaction parameters stay fixed, which connects the model's
$D$ and $B$ sectors, or its $D_s$ and $B_s$ sectors, or --- varying both masses
--- charmonium and bottomonium. Subtracting the constituent rest masses
separates the change in binding and excitation structure from the plain rise in
total mass, and hyperfine splittings, level ordering, and the response of the
light degrees of freedom become things to watch rather than tabulate. The
interpolation is a family of model calculations, not a physical transition
between flavors.

The same access to wavefunctions supports structure pictures: radial densities,
nodes, characteristic radii, angular distributions, and the components of a
mixed state. These are interpretable as long as they say what they display ---
for the normalized reduced radial wave $u(r)=rR(r)$, $|u(r)|^2\,dr$ is a
radial probability, while the three-dimensional density
$|R_{nL}(r)\,Y_{Lm}(\theta,\phi)|^2$ carries the angular factor as well. The
ingredients for a curated meson-structure animation are in place as well; the
animation itself is not yet. `Fig.~\ref{fig:structure}`{=latex} is where those pictures
belong.


# Conclusion and outlook {#sec-conclusion}

The GI spectrum can be regenerated from the published ingredients alone, by the
paper's own three-stage algorithm, with an independent numerical route agreeing
with it, and the calculation can now be inspected operator by operator instead
of being reconstructed privately each time it is needed. The open work is the
photon-decay coverage and the cancellation-sensitive observables that go with
it.

The natural continuations are physics rather than software. Screened
interactions [@li2009] and explicit coupled-channel treatments
[@barnes2008; @ortega2010] are the directions in which the GI baseline has
mostly been extended, and each changes the model and needs its own validation.
Closer to hand, the quark-emission operator behind the paper's strong-decay
analysis can be applied directly to the calculated physical wavefunctions,
instead of the single-oscillator-scale approximation used for its numerical
tables, which would expose
the role of radial nodes, state-dependent scales, and mixing in those
amplitudes. That is the test I most want to run, because it uses the
wavefunctions rather than only the eigenvalues.

Julia makes one further direction tempting. For an isolated normalized
eigenstate, the Hellmann--Feynman relation
```{=latex}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hellmann}
\frac{\partial E_n}{\partial\lambda}
 =\left\langle\psi_n\left|
 \frac{\partial H}{\partial\lambda}\right|\psi_n\right\rangle
\end{equation}
```
is an explicit starting point for sensitivity studies and fitting, and the
repository already contains the numerical-type preparation and FD and
fixed-scale HO derivative probes. End-to-end automatic differentiation is
future work, and not trivially so: adaptive basis selection, level crossings,
and derivatives of mixed eigenvectors all need care.

If the project has a moral, it is the one from @sec-implementation: the model
became clear at exactly the points where the code was confidently wrong. That
is the experience the course and the notebooks are meant to make available to
someone else --- ask a question, get a number, take the number apart, and find
out what you had assumed.
